headline: KKR: record fee earnings up 27% and a $2 billion gain coming from the USI sale, as the firm returns record cash to clients
takeaway: Adjusted net income rose 29% to $1.78 a share, beating the $1.58 consensus, and fee-related earnings rose 27% to a record $1.3 billion. KKR expects the sale of USI Insurance Services to add about $2 billion, or more than $2 a share, in the fourth quarter, and raised its buyback by $500 million.
results: KKR reported adjusted net income of $1.6 billion, or $1.78 per adjusted share, for the third quarter, up 29% from a year earlier and above analysts’ $1.58. Fee-related earnings — the steady management and transaction fees that investors value most — were $1.3 billion, or $1.42 a share, up 27%. Total operating earnings, which add the insurance business and recurring income from strategic holdings, rose 25% to $1.88 a share. All three per-share figures were records for KKR as a public company.

Insurance operating earnings at Global Atlantic were $230 million, including a $26 million charge from its annual actuarial review; excluding it they would have been $257 million. GAAP net income attributable to common shareholders was $1.1 billion.

Assets under management reached $804 billion, up 11%, and fee-paying assets $648 billion, also up 11%. KKR raised $25 billion of new capital in the quarter and $116 billion over twelve months, invested $20 billion, and has $146 billion of uncommitted dry powder plus $75 billion of committed capital that will start paying fees, at about 0.9%, once invested.
mgmt: Co-chief executives Joseph Bae and Scott Nuttall said KKR is monetising investments and returning capital to clients at record levels and expects to return more than $40 billion in 2026, more than 50% above its previous annual record. Of $415 billion of carry-eligible assets, $332 billion is above cost and accruing carried interest.

KKR agreed in August to sell USI Insurance Services, the first investment in its Core Private Equity strategy, and expects the deal to close in the fourth quarter and generate about $2.0 billion of adjusted net income. The firm bought back 6.2 million shares at an average of $92, raised its repurchase programme by $500 million and declared a regular dividend of $0.195.
view: The private-equity industry spent 2023 to 2025 unable to sell what it owned: high rates and a shut IPO market left funds sitting on companies, clients waiting for cash and fundraising stalled. This quarter is the clearest evidence yet that the logjam has broken at KKR. Returning more than $40 billion to clients in a year matters for two reasons — it crystallises carried interest for KKR’s own shareholders, and clients who get cash back recommit it to the next fund, which feeds future fee growth.

The quality of the beat is high. Fee-related earnings growing 27% is not a markets windfall but the result of a decade of building insurance, credit, infrastructure and private-wealth businesses that charge fees on permanent or long-dated capital. The $75 billion of committed capital not yet paying fees is effectively contracted future revenue of roughly $675 million a year. The USI sale is a one-off, but a very instructive one: Core Private Equity was KKR’s bet that holding businesses for 15 years or more could compound value for its own balance sheet, and a $2 billion gain on the first exit is a strong validation.

The risks are the ones the whole sector shares. Private credit has grown so fast that any rise in defaults would hit both fees and Global Atlantic’s investment portfolio, and the push into retail and 401(k) money brings regulatory and reputational exposure. KKR’s share price, around $92 at the buyback and lower since, already discounts more than it did a year ago, but at roughly 15 times trailing adjusted earnings for a business growing fee income at more than 25%, this report argues the market is still treating KKR as a cyclical dealmaker rather than an asset manager with rising recurring income.
watch: Watch the closing of the USI sale and the size of fourth-quarter realisations, fundraising for the next flagship buyout and infrastructure funds, and credit quality in the private-credit and insurance portfolios.
